property_summary: After calling getFirstWithdrawalBonus(recipient) the recipient's balance increases by exactly 100 wei and c.rewardsForA(recipient) becomes 0 (so contract balance decreases by 100), because withdrawReward always succeeds on the original but may revert with transfer in the mutant.
Calling withdrawReward should never succeed (i.e., must revert) when the recipient is a contract that rejects plain transfers while P uses low-level call allowing failure to be observed as revert.
For the given recipient, calling c.withdrawReward(recipient) must revert (reverted == true).
For the given recipient address, calling c.withdrawReward(recipient) must revert (reverted == true).
For the given recipient, calling c.withdrawReward(recipient) must revert (reverted == true).

For any recipient, calling getFirstWithdrawalBonus(recipient) on the correct contract always completes successfully and leaves rewardsForA[recipient] == 0 (no leftover withdrawable balance), but replacing the low-level call with transfer can cause the external send to revert for some malicious recipient, making getFirstWithdrawalBonus revert (and thus violating the always-completes rule / leaving state unchanged across the call boundary).

For any recipient, calling getFirstWithdrawalBonus(recipient) on the correct contract always completes (does not revert) even if the recipient's fallback reverts, because the reference uses a low-level call and checks its return; the mutant that uses transfer will revert when the recipient's receive/fallback reverts, breaking that universal non-revert property for some adversarial recipient contract.

For every recipient contract whose fallback/receive may revert, the reference C ensures that getFirstWithdrawalBonus(recipient) either succeeds and leaves rewardsForA[recipient]==0 OR, if the external send fails, the reference reverts only after reverting internal state to the pre-call state (so no partial side-effect: claimedBonus[recipient] remains false and rewardsForA[recipient] unchanged); the mutant using transfer can cause an unconditional revert that prevents the reference's tolerant behavior and thus observable differences (we assert that after calling getFirstWithdrawalBonus on the reference via a reverting recipient helper, the call does not mark claimedBonus and leaves rewardsForA unchanged).

After calling withdrawReward(recipient), the reference contract always resets rewardsForA[recipient] to zero (so address(c).balance decreases by that amount and subsequent getter shows 0); the mutant that zeros after the external call can be re-entered to observe a nonzero rewardsForA and thus violates this invariant for some attacker and amount.
